title: mesh-aware-activation-router-and-quantized-kv-ops
content:
Purpose:
This doc sketches a pragmatic design for an activation routing layer that is aware of multi-GPU mesh topology and pairs it with a compact, quantization-first KV op pipeline. Goal is to reduce cross-host NCCL pressure for common short-sequence workloads while preserving tail-latency SLOs for interactive inference.

Context and motivation:
- We serve mixed workloads: chat (short context, high qps), long-form generation (large context, lower qps), and retrieval-augmented patterns that touch embeddings and KV cache differently.
- Current sharding heuristics aim to minimize total bytes moved, but they are agnostic to runtime mesh congestion patterns and quantized-memory layout. We see periodic NCCL stalls on certain topology shapes (heterogeneous subracks, uneven p2p speeds) and excessive PCIe/host-copy when legacy KV operations trigger full-precision activation exchanges.
- Hypothesis: A lightweight router that picks activation routes (intra-node, intra-rack, cross-rack) per request and a companion set of quantized KV op kernels will cut interconnect utilization and cost while keeping end-to-end latency predictable.

Requirements and success metrics:
- Latency: 95th percentile token latency should not regress by more than 5% for latency-sensitive routes.
- Throughput: Overall tokens/sec across the fleet should improve by >= 8% for mixed short-sequence workloads in experiments.
- Cost: Measurable reduction in cross-host NCCL-bw (GiB/s) during peak by >= 12% in target configs.
- Correctness: No model degradation; outputs identical (bit-for-bit) for FP32 paths; quantized paths must be validated with eval sets and have clear quality metrics.

Constraints:
- Must interoperate with existing model partitioning (tensor-parallel + pipeline-parallel) without forcing a full reshard.
- Changes should be runtime-only where possible (config flags, kernel registry) to facilitate staged rollout to Dedicated and Private customers.
- Quantized KV must support common quant formats (int8/4bit symmetric, DP4A-ready layouts) and fast dequant path for final logits where required.

Design overview:
1) Activation Router (AR): lightweight decision plane that assigns each request to an activation route per layer boundary. Decisions use small feature vectors: request context length, model variant id, current per-link congestion score, and per-GPU free memory headroom. AR operates in two modes: static (policy from compile-time heuristics) and adaptive (hot-path uses realtime telemetry).

2) Route types:
- local: keep activation tensors on same GPU when kernel allows (no transfer).
- intra-node: use NVLink or fast PCIe within the same host (NCCL OOB optimizations achievable).
- intra-rack: favor top-of-rack NVSwitch/NIC if available; aggregate ops to reduce chatty small-collectives.
- cross-rack: last resort; use bandwidth-aware collective plans with compression/quantization.

3) Per-layer routing granularity:
- router can pick per-layer or per-stage strategies. For small matrix multiplies in attention (q/k/v projection), prefer local/intra-node; for large feed-forward blocks that exceed local memory, allow split with scheduled asynchronous host-offload.

4) Quantized KV ops library:
- KV store layout: compact row-major with chunked key/value segments aligned to 64B for DMA. Per-shard metadata stores scale/zero for each chunk so dequant is local to the consumer.
- Insertion/lookup kernels: two variants — fast-read (no-dequant; return compressed bytes across NCCL) and eager-dequant (dequant on producer GPU before send). Choice depends on route: cross-rack prefers compressed bytes + dequant-on-receive to reduce wire size.
- Backup-path: always provide an FP fallback kernel to run the same op when quantization is disabled or for certain critical eval traffic.

5) NCCL and collective tuning:
- Small-collective fusion: router accumulates many small KV exchanges within a short window (configurable microbatch) and issues a single fused NCCL allgather when beneficial. This reduces kernel-launch overhead and handshake noise for chatty workloads.
- Topology hints: scheduler consumes topology map (p2p bandwidth matrix) and biases tree-based collectives to prefer high-bandwidth links and avoid slow cross-links. We will integrate this as a NCCL plan filter rather than a NCCL patch to keep upgrades simple.
- Adaptive fallback: detect high-latency collectives (per-call RTT > threshold) and shift route plan to more local/serialized ops for the next N requests for that session.

Scheduling heuristics and policy:
- Cost model: estimate cost of a route as alpha * expected-wire-bytes / bw + beta * extra-latency + gamma * remote-GPU-load. We will learn alpha/beta/gamma via offline regression from A/B experiments.
- Priority classes: latency-sensitive (interactive), throughput-oriented (batch), and mixed. Router policy table maps model + request class -> preferred route profile.
- Safety caps: prevent router from sending > X% cross-rack traffic from a single host in a time window to avoid thrashing.

Implementation sketch:
- New components:
  * ar-agent: small C++ service per-worker exposing a sync API for per-request route decisions; hot-path optimized (inlined decisions using shared mem telemetry).
  * kv-qkernels: CUDA + vectorized CPU kernels for int8/4bit pack/unpack, fused dequant+gemm-ready layout transforms.
  * metric hooks: per-collective latency, bytes, congestion counters; route decisions annotated in traces (span tag).
- Config: runtime flags to toggle fusion windows, quantization format, per-route policies, and threshold for adaptive fallback.
- Rollout: feature-gated in Canary -> Region -> Fleet. Start with non-production traffic (eval harness) then low-risk customer tiers.

Experiment matrix and eval plan:
- A/B cluster experiments across three topology types: homogeneous NVLink-full rack, mixed NVLink+PCIe nodes, and cross-rack staged cluster. Each experiment measures P50/P95/P99 token latency, NCCL bw, host CPU overhead, and model output divergence (for quant paths).
- Microbenchmarks: per-layer activation transfer sizes and per-collective latency under varying aggregation windows.
- Quality: run standard eval suite (translation/LLM QA/CoQA) and embedding drift tests. Set automatic alerts for regression > tolerance.

Operational considerations:
- Telemetry: extend per-request trace context to include chosen route and quant mode. Dashboards: route distribution, cross-rack bytes, fused-collective frequency, per-route p95s.
- Debugging: 'force-route' toggle to reproduce issues and 'trace-replay' harness to simulate a sequence using recorded telemetry for offline analysis.
- Security: quantized bytes on wire are treated as sensitive; preserve existing encryption-in-transit and KMS policies. Quantization metadata must be access-controlled.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- How aggressive can we quantize KV values without measurable downstream output drift? We need a progressive calibration plan per-model and per-workload.
- Fusion window vs latency tradeoff: what is the optimal microbatch window for chatty workloads? This likely depends on arrival distribution; consider an adaptive window that targets a per-GPU microbatch size.
- Integration with pipeline-parallel schedule: per-layer routing could complicate current pipeline bubble scheduling. We must ensure routing decisions do not increase pipeline stalls or memory fragmentation.

Next steps / TODOs:
- Prototype ar-agent and a minimal int8 KV read/pack kernel (2 engineer sprint).
- Add topology sampler to our test harness to simulate bad-links and validate adaptive fallback logic (1 sprint).
- Run internal A/B against canary subset (5% traffic) with detailed telemetry capture.
- Work with SRE to define SLO guardrails for cross-rack bytes and rollout automation.

Appendix: quick pseudo-workflow example:
- Ingress request arrives for chat session (ctx_len=32). Dispatcher asks ar-agent for route for layer L.
- ar-agent consults local congestion counters, sees intra-node NVLink free. Picks 'intra-node+fused' route.
- KV lookup uses fast-read compressed path; returns compressed chunks via fused NCCL allgather. Dequant happens on consumer GPU and execution continues.

References and prior artifacts:
- Related notes: scattered-kv-coherence-playbook, scatter-gather-kv-coherence-playbook (see shared folder).
- Linked GH/JIRA/Confluence entries in header for implementation traceability.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally implementation-focused and runtime-first. We want feedback on the safety caps, the proposed per-request decision cost model, and whether per-layer routing granularity is too fine-grained for pipeline integration.
